The slight degradation in reliability (0.82→0.73 test-retest Likert) suggests possible domain-specific effects that are not fully understood.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) as a structured alternative to traditional textual summaries, supported by a novel low-context importance annotation crowdsourcing scheme and a 30-topic corpus with ~40 documents each. The work makes four main contributions: (1) task definition for concept-map-based MDS with extractive constraints, (2) a novel crowdsourcing methodology (low-context importance annotation) that reduces task complexity while maintaining reasonable reliability (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement), (3) a gold-standard corpus created via hybrid pipeline combining automatic preprocessing (Open IE 4), crowdsourcing (53k Likert + 12k comparison tasks), and expert annotation (3 annotators, κ=0.66-0.70), and (4) evaluation protocol with three automatic metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) and baseline system. The corpus represents a substantial resource contribution with large-scale heterogeneous document clusters (97,880 tokens per cluster, 15× larger than DUC) across diverse genres (28% professional, 26% educational, 16% personal blogs, 12% forums, 12% link collections, 6% scientific). The paper demonstrates methodological rigor in resource creation but exhibits critical gaps in validating core conceptual claims and evaluation approaches. The core motivation claim (concept maps are more natural than textual summaries) relies entirely on prior user studies without direct empirical validation within this work. Automatic evaluation metrics are proposed but not validated against human judgments. The baseline system is intentionally simple, making it difficult to assess true task difficulty. The corpus is limited to educational topics, and generalizability to other domains is not addressed.
strengths: Novel crowdsourcing methodology with empirical validation: Low-context importance annotation is well-motivated, addresses documented quality issues in prior work (Lloret et al., 2013), and shows reasonable reliability (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement on full corpus) with cost-effectiveness ($4425.45 for 65k tasks). Pilot study on TAC data (0.81 Likert, 0.73 comparison) demonstrates viability despite minimal context.

Substantial corpus with large-scale heterogeneous document clusters: 30 topics with ~40 documents each (97,880 tokens per cluster, 15× larger than DUC) across diverse genres (28% professional, 26% educational, 16% personal blogs, 12% forums, 12% link collections, 6% scientific) with high textual heterogeneity (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.3490 vs. 0.3019 in DUC 2004). Represents significant resource contribution with clear advantages over prior concept map corpora.

Transparent and pragmatic corpus creation pipeline: Well-documented hybrid pipeline combining automatic preprocessing (Open IE 4: 4137→2850 tuples), crowdsourcing (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement), and expert annotation (κ=0.66-0.70). Detailed error analysis at each step (76% concept coverage in extraction, 17% in top-25 selection) identifies bottlenecks. Pragmatic acknowledgment of constraints (0.77 synthetic relations per map when extractive constraint cannot be met).

Comprehensive corpus characterization and task difficulty analysis: Detailed comparison to traditional MDS benchmarks (DUC, TAC) on cluster size, document length variability, genre diversity, and textual heterogeneity. Baseline system analysis identifies specific bottlenecks in content selection and relation extraction, demonstrating task is substantially more challenging than traditional MDS.

Clear task definition with explicit constraints: Well-defined concept-map-based MDS task with extractive variant, 25-concept size limit (justified by Novak & Cañas 2007), and connectedness requirement. Enables reproducible research and comparable evaluation.
limitations: Core motivation claim (C1: concept maps are more natural than textual summaries) relies entirely on prior user studies (Chin et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2011) about human note-taking behavior, not direct validation within this work. No user study compares utility, comprehension, or preference for concept maps vs. textual summaries on the same document clusters. The connection between note-taking behavior and utility of concept maps as summaries is inferred but not empirically validated. This is a critical gap for a paper proposing a novel task variant.

Automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) are proposed but not validated against human judgments of concept map quality. The metrics treat concept maps as sets of propositions (concatenated strings) and do not capture graph structure (connectivity, hierarchy, centrality), which may be important for concept map quality. Without human evaluation, it is unclear whether these metrics correlate with human assessments or capture important quality dimensions. This is a major gap for a resource paper intended to enable system development.

Test-retest reliability for comparison tasks (0.69 pilot, 0.72 full corpus) is notably lower than for Likert tasks (0.82 pilot, 0.73 full corpus), suggesting comparison tasks may be less reliable. The reason for this 10-13 percentage point discrepancy is not explained or investigated. This raises questions about the reliability of importance rankings derived from comparison tasks and their impact on corpus quality.

Corpus is limited to educational topics from DIP corpus; generalizability to other domains (news, scientific, medical, legal) is not addressed despite being listed as an evaluation dimension. No evaluation on other domains is conducted. This limits the broader impact and applicability of the corpus creation methodology.

Baseline system is intentionally simple (NP extraction, stemming-based merging, heuristic relation extraction, Random Forest ranking) and may not represent state-of-the-art difficulty. Low baseline performance (17% concept coverage in top-25 selection) could reflect implementation limitations rather than inherent task difficulty. No comparison to stronger baselines or state-of-the-art methods is provided, making it difficult to assess true task difficulty.
open_questions: How would users actually prefer to interact with concept-map vs. textual summaries for information seeking on large document collections? Would concept maps improve comprehension, information retention, or task completion time compared to textual summaries? A user study directly comparing these representations on the same document clusters would validate the core motivation and provide empirical evidence for the task formulation.

Do the proposed automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) correlate with human judgments of concept map quality? What aspects of quality do these metrics capture or miss? Would graph-aware metrics (e.g., based on graph edit distance, connectivity measures, centrality) better capture concept map quality? Human evaluation of concept maps would validate the evaluation protocol and guide metric improvements.

Why is test-retest reliability for comparison tasks (0.72) substantially lower than for Likert tasks (0.73)? Is this due to task design (drag-and-drop interface), worker behavior (inconsistency in pairwise judgments), or the TrueSkill ranking model (noise amplification)? Investigation of this discrepancy would improve understanding of crowdsourcing reliability and inform task design for future work.

Does the corpus creation methodology generalize to other domains beyond educational topics? Would low-context importance annotation work equally well for news, scientific, medical, or legal documents? Would the SVM classifier for proposition filtering trained on educational topics generalize to other domains? Pilot studies on different domains would assess generalizability and broaden the applicability of the methodology.

What is the cumulative error rate through the corpus creation pipeline? How do errors in proposition extraction (Open IE 4) propagate through SVM filtering, crowdsourcing, and expert annotation? Which types of errors (false positives, false negatives, incorrect argument boundaries) have the largest impact on final corpus quality? Error propagation analysis would improve understanding of corpus quality and identify opportunities for pipeline improvements.

How would stronger baselines using neural methods (BERT-based importance scoring, graph neural networks for relation extraction) perform on this task? Would they achieve substantially higher performance than the simple baseline, suggesting the task is less challenging than claimed? Comparison to state-of-the-art methods would better characterize task difficulty and identify promising research directions.

Is the fixed 25-concept size limit appropriate for all topics? Do topics of varying complexity require different summary sizes? Would allowing variable-size concept maps (e.g., 20-30 concepts) improve information coverage without sacrificing quality? Analysis of topic complexity and coverage would inform optimal summary size selection.
consensus_snapshot: Low-context importance annotation is a viable and cost-effective crowdsourcing methodology with reasonable reliability (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement) that addresses documented quality issues in prior work (Lloret et al., 2013). Pilot validation on TAC data demonstrates viability, though test-retest correlation for comparison tasks is notably lower than Likert tasks.

The corpus represents a substantial resource contribution with large-scale heterogeneous document clusters (97,880 tokens per cluster, 15× larger than DUC) across diverse genres. The corpus creation pipeline is well-documented with transparent quality checkpoints and error analysis.

Expert annotation agreement is substantial but not perfect (κ=0.66-0.70), based on a limited sample (3 annotators, 3 maps). The inter-annotator disagreement on proposition selection (κ=0.66) is only moderate, suggesting non-trivial annotation difficulty.

The extractive task definition is partially violated by 0.77 synthetic relations per map (freely defined labels) when extractive constraint cannot be met. The impact of this violation on task definition clarity and evaluation metric validity is not analyzed.

Automatic evaluation metrics are proposed but not validated against human judgments. The metrics do not capture graph structure (connectivity, hierarchy), which may be important for concept map quality.
The baseline system is intentionally simple and may not represent state-of-the-art difficulty. Low baseline performance could reflect implementation limitations rather than inherent task difficulty.
disagreement_snapshot: Novelty assessment: Reviewers characterize the work differently on the novelty spectrum. Structure_analyst and methodology_auditor view it as incremental with solid methodological contributions. Novelty_assessors identify genuine innovation in task formulation and resource contribution. The disagreement reflects different perspectives on whether task reformulation (concept-map-based MDS) constitutes novelty or incremental extension.

Task difficulty claim: Reviewers differ on confidence in the task difficulty claim (C4). Some emphasize corpus characteristics (15× larger clusters, heterogeneous genres) as evidence of difficulty. Others note that the simple baseline may not reflect true difficulty and that stronger baselines could reduce apparent challenge.

Generalizability of low-context importance annotation: Reviewers differ in severity assessment of domain transfer from TAC (news) to educational topics. Some flag this as a methodological concern requiring investigation. Others treat it as a minor uncertainty or pragmatic limitation.

Significance of test-retest reliability discrepancy: All reviewers note the lower test-retest correlation for comparison tasks (0.69-0.72) vs. Likert tasks (0.73-0.82), but differ in severity assessment. Some treat this as a moderate concern requiring investigation; others identify it as a methodological flaw affecting reliability of importance annotations.
uncertainty_snapshot: Core motivation validation: The claim that concept maps are more natural than textual summaries relies on prior user studies about note-taking behavior, not direct validation within this work. No user study compares utility, comprehension, or preference for concept maps vs. textual summaries on the same document clusters. This is flagged as a major gap by multiple reviewers.

Automatic evaluation metric validity: The three proposed metrics are not validated against human judgments of concept map quality. The metrics treat concept maps as proposition sets and do not capture graph structure (connectivity, hierarchy), which may be important for quality assessment. This is flagged as a major methodological flaw.

Generalization of corpus creation methodology: The corpus is limited to educational topics, and generalizability to other domains (news, scientific, medical) is not addressed despite being listed as an evaluation dimension. This is flagged as a moderate concern.

Error propagation through corpus creation pipeline: The pipeline introduces cumulative errors (Open IE extraction, SVM filtering with 5.6% manual correction rate, crowdsourcing, expert annotation) but error propagation is not fully analyzed. This is flagged as a moderate concern.

Test-retest reliability discrepancy for comparison tasks: The reason for lower test-retest correlation for comparison tasks (0.69-0.72) compared to Likert tasks (0.73-0.82) is unexplained. This is flagged as requiring investigation.

Baseline system strength: The simple baseline may not reflect true task difficulty. Stronger baselines using neural methods could achieve higher performance, suggesting the task may be less challenging than claimed. This is flagged as a moderate concern.

Fixed concept map size (25 concepts): The fixed size limit may not be appropriate for all topics of varying complexity. No analysis of size variation by topic complexity is provided. This is flagged as a low-confidence concern.
source_trace: Claim C1 (concept maps are more natural): Introduction (lines 011-048) cites Chin et al. (2009) and Kang et al. (2011) for user behavior evidence; no direct validation within this work.

Claim C2 (low-context importance annotation viable): Section 3 (lines 201-399) reports pilot study on TAC2008 (0.81 Likert, 0.73 comparison agreement) and full corpus results (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement, 0.73 test-retest Likert, 0.72 comparison).

Claim C3 (corpus creation via hybrid pipeline): Section 4 (lines 401-699) documents 5-step pipeline: Open IE extraction (4137→2850 tuples), SVM filtering (93% precision, 955 manual corrections), crowdsourced importance annotation (53k Likert + 12k comparison tasks), expert annotation (3 annotators, κ=0.66-0.70), concept map construction (25 concepts, 24-28 relations, 0.77 synthetic relations per map).

Claim C4 (task substantially more challenging): Section 5 (lines 701-799) compares corpus characteristics to DUC/TAC: cluster size 97,880 vs. 17,461 (DUC 2006), document length variability 1.56 vs. 0.74-0.82, genre diversity (28% professional, 26% educational, 16% personal blogs, 12% forums, 12% link collections, 6% scientific), textual heterogeneity (JS divergence 0.3490 vs. 0.3019 DUC 2004).

Claim C5 (automatic metrics adapted for concept maps): Section 6 (lines 801-899) proposes Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2; baseline achieves 76% concept coverage in extraction, 17% in top-25 selection, low strict match scores.

Test-retest reliability discrepancy: Section 3.2 (lines 356-399) reports pilot study test-retest 0.82 Likert vs. 0.69 comparison; Section 4.4 (lines 401-449) reports full corpus test-retest 0.73 Likert vs. 0.72 comparison. No explanation provided.
Inter-annotator agreement limited sample: Section 4.6 (lines 601-699) states 'we had the first three maps created by two annotators' for agreement study; only 3 topics used for κ computation.

Synthetic relations violating extractive constraint: Section 4.6 (lines 601-699) states 'allowed to create up to three synthetic relations with freely defined labels'; average 0.77 synthetic relations per map reported.
Automatic metrics not validated: Section 6 (lines 801-899) proposes metrics but provides no human evaluation or correlation analysis with human judgments.
Corpus limited to educational topics: Section 4.1 (lines 401-425) uses 30 of 49 topics from DIP corpus (educational topics); no evaluation on other domains.

Baseline simplicity: Section 6 (lines 801-899) describes baseline as 'simple approach inspired by previous work'; uses NP extraction, stemming-based merging, heuristic relation extraction, Random Forest ranking; no comparison to stronger baselines.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about methodology and corpus creation pipeline, with clear documentation of quality checkpoints and error analysis at each step. The paper acknowledges pragmatic compromises (e.g., allowing synthetic relations when extractive constraint cannot be met) and documents their rationale.

The paper provides detailed inter-annotator agreement statistics (κ=0.66-0.70) and crowdsourcing reliability metrics (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement), though the limited sample for agreement study (3 annotators, 3 maps) is not explicitly acknowledged as a limitation.

The paper does not explicitly discuss limitations of core motivation claim (C1) or acknowledge that it relies on prior user studies without direct validation in this work. The core motivation is presented as established fact rather than as a hypothesis requiring validation.

The paper does not discuss generalizability limitations or acknowledge that the corpus is limited to educational topics despite listing generalizability as an evaluation dimension. The limitation to educational topics is not explicitly stated as a constraint.
The paper does not validate automatic evaluation metrics against human judgments or acknowledge this as a gap. The metrics are proposed without discussion of their validity or limitations.

The paper does not provide a direct comparison of concept maps to textual summaries or acknowledge this as a gap. The core motivation relies on prior user studies about note-taking behavior rather than direct preference studies.

The paper does not explain the lower test-retest correlation for comparison tasks (0.69-0.72) compared to Likert tasks (0.73-0.82). This discrepancy is noted in results but not discussed or investigated.

The paper does not analyze error propagation through the corpus creation pipeline, despite documenting error rates at individual steps. The cumulative impact of errors on final corpus quality is not assessed.

The paper is transparent about the simplicity of the baseline system but does not discuss implications for task difficulty assessment. The low baseline performance is attributed to task difficulty without considering baseline limitations.

The paper is transparent about the domain transfer from TAC (news) to educational topics, noting that full corpus reliability is slightly lower than pilot study, but does not explicitly discuss implications for generalizability.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes solid contributions to NLP infrastructure (task definition, corpus, crowdsourcing methodology) and should be evaluated primarily as a resource contribution rather than a conceptual or algorithmic innovation. The work demonstrates methodological rigor in corpus creation but exhibits critical gaps in validating core conceptual claims and evaluation approaches. Key decision points: (1) The core motivation claim (concept maps are more natural than textual summaries) relies entirely on prior user studies without direct validation in this work. This is a significant gap for a paper proposing a novel task variant, but not necessarily disqualifying if the work is framed as enabling future research on this question. (2) Automatic evaluation metrics are proposed but not validated against human judgments. This is a critical gap for a resource paper, as it undermines the utility of the corpus for system development. (3) The corpus is limited to educational topics; generalizability to other domains is not addressed. This limits the broader impact of the work. (4) The baseline system is simple; stronger baselines would better characterize task difficulty. (5) The low-context importance annotation shows reasonable reliability (0.80 Likert agreement) but with notable degradation in test-retest correlation for comparison tasks (0.72 vs. 0.82 Likert). The reason for this discrepancy should be investigated. Recommendation: The paper makes sufficient contributions to warrant publication as a resource paper, but should be revised to: (1) Acknowledge limitations of core motivation claim and frame as enabling future research; (2) Conduct human evaluation of automatic metrics or acknowledge this as future work; (3) Discuss generalizability limitations and recommend domain-specific evaluation; (4) Implement stronger baselines or acknowledge baseline limitations; (5) Investigate and explain test-retest reliability discrepancy for comparison tasks. The work should not be rejected based on lack of user validation of core motivation, as this is a common limitation in resource papers. However, the lack of metric validation is a more serious concern that should be addressed before publication.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: The paper makes valuable contributions to NLP infrastructure and should be strengthened by addressing the following gaps: (1) Core motivation validation: Conduct a user study comparing concept maps to textual summaries on a subset of the corpus, measuring utility, comprehension, and preference. If this is not feasible, explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation and frame the work as enabling future research on this question. (2) Automatic metric validation: Conduct human evaluation of concept maps generated by the baseline system, measuring correlation between automatic metrics and human judgments. Consider developing graph-aware metrics that capture connectivity and hierarchy. (3) Generalizability: Discuss limitations of corpus to educational topics and recommend future work on other domains. If possible, conduct pilot studies on news or scientific topics to assess generalizability of the corpus creation methodology. (4) Baseline strength: Implement stronger baselines using neural methods (BERT-based importance scoring, graph neural networks for relation extraction) and compare performance. Conduct ablation studies to identify which baseline components are most limiting. (5) Test-retest reliability: Investigate and explain the lower test-retest correlation for comparison tasks (0.72 vs. 0.82 Likert). Consider whether comparison tasks should be weighted differently or used only for top-ranked propositions. (6) Error propagation: Analyze error propagation through the corpus creation pipeline by computing precision/recall at each step and tracing sample propositions through the pipeline. (7) Extractive task definition: Clarify whether the task is extractive or hybrid (mostly extractive with limited abstractive relations). If hybrid, update task definition and evaluation protocol accordingly. (8) Inter-annotator agreement: Expand agreement study to include at least 10% of corpus (3 additional maps, 9 total) with confidence intervals. Analyze sources of disagreement and provide guidelines for resolving disagreements. (9) Fixed concept map size: Analyze whether 25 concepts is appropriate for all topics by examining topic complexity and coverage. Consider allowing variable map sizes within a range. (10) Synthetic relations: Analyze distribution of synthetic relations across topics and discuss whether they compromise the extractive constraint. Consider whether synthetic relations should be excluded from evaluation or treated separately.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) as a structured alternative to traditional textual summaries. The work combines four contributions: (1) a novel task definition with extractive constraints, (2) a low-context importance annotation crowdsourcing scheme, (3) a 30-topic corpus with gold-standard concept maps created via hybrid pipeline, and (4) evaluation protocol with automatic metrics and baseline system. The corpus features large-scale heterogeneous document clusters (97,880 tokens per cluster, 15× larger than DUC) across diverse genres (28% professional, 26% educational, 16% personal blogs, 12% forums, 12% link collections, 6% scientific). The paper demonstrates methodological rigor in resource creation but exhibits critical gaps in validating core conceptual claims and evaluation approaches.

Strengths:
- Novel crowdsourcing methodology with empirical validation: Low-context importance annotation is well-motivated, addresses documented quality issues in prior work (Lloret et al., 2013), and shows reasonable reliability (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement on full corpus) with cost-effectiveness ($4425.45 for 65k tasks). Pilot study on TAC data (0.81 Likert, 0.73 comparison) demonstrates viability despite minimal context.
- Substantial corpus with large-scale heterogeneous document clusters: 30 topics with ~40 documents each (97,880 tokens per cluster, 15× larger than DUC) across diverse genres with high textual heterogeneity (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.3490 vs. 0.3019 in DUC 2004). Represents significant resource contribution with clear advantages over prior concept map corpora.
- Transparent and pragmatic corpus creation pipeline: Well-documented hybrid pipeline combining automatic preprocessing (Open IE 4: 4137→2850 tuples), crowdsourcing (0.80 Likert, 0.78 comparison agreement), and expert annotation (κ=0.66-0.70). Detailed error analysis at each step identifies bottlenecks (76% concept coverage in extraction, 17% in top-25 selection).
- Comprehensive corpus characterization and task difficulty analysis: Detailed comparison to traditional MDS benchmarks (DUC, TAC) on cluster size, document length variability, genre diversity, and textual heterogeneity. Baseline system analysis identifies specific bottlenecks in content selection and relation extraction.
- Clear task definition with explicit constraints: Well-defined concept-map-based MDS task with extractive variant, 25-concept size limit (justified by Novak & Cañas 2007), and connectedness requirement. Enables reproducible research and comparable evaluation.

Limitations:
- Core motivation claim (C1: concept maps are more natural than textual summaries) relies entirely on prior user studies (Chin et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2011) about human note-taking behavior, not direct validation within this work. No user study compares utility, comprehension, or preference for concept maps vs. textual summaries on the same document clusters. The connection between note-taking behavior and utility of concept maps as summaries is inferred but not empirically validated. This is a critical gap for a paper proposing a novel task variant.
- Automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) are proposed but not validated against human judgments of concept map quality. The metrics treat concept maps as sets of propositions (concatenated strings) and do not capture graph structure (connectivity, hierarchy, centrality), which may be important for concept map quality. Without human evaluation, it is unclear whether these metrics correlate with human assessments or capture important quality dimensions. This is a major gap for a resource paper intended to enable system development.
- Test-retest reliability for comparison tasks (0.69 pilot, 0.72 full corpus) is notably lower than for Likert tasks (0.82 pilot, 0.73 full corpus), suggesting comparison tasks may be less reliable. The reason for this 10-13 percentage point discrepancy is not explained or investigated. This raises questions about the reliability of importance rankings derived from comparison tasks and their impact on corpus quality.
- Corpus is limited to educational topics from DIP corpus; generalizability to other domains (news, scientific, medical, legal) is not addressed despite being listed as an evaluation dimension. No evaluation on other domains is conducted. This limits the broader impact and applicability of the corpus creation methodology.
- Baseline system is intentionally simple (NP extraction, stemming-based merging, heuristic relation extraction, Random Forest ranking) and may not represent state-of-the-art difficulty. Low baseline performance (17% concept coverage in top-25 selection) could reflect implementation limitations rather than inherent task difficulty. No comparison to stronger baselines or state-of-the-art methods is provided, making it difficult to assess true task difficulty.

Open Questions:
- How would users actually prefer to interact with concept-map vs. textual summaries for information seeking on large document collections? Would concept maps improve comprehension, information retention, or task completion time compared to textual summaries? A user study directly comparing these representations on the same document clusters would validate the core motivation and provide empirical evidence for the task formulation.
- Do the proposed automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) correlate with human judgments of concept map quality? What aspects of quality do these metrics capture or miss? Would graph-aware metrics (e.g., based on graph edit distance, connectivity measures, centrality) better capture concept map quality? Human evaluation of concept maps would validate the evaluation protocol and guide metric improvements.
- Why is test-retest reliability for comparison tasks (0.72) substantially lower than for Likert tasks (0.73)? Is this due to task design (drag-and-drop interface), worker behavior (inconsistency in pairwise judgments), or the TrueSkill ranking model (noise amplification)? Investigation of this discrepancy would improve understanding of crowdsourcing reliability and inform task design for future work.
- Does the corpus creation methodology generalize to other domains beyond educational topics? Would low-context importance annotation work equally well for news, scientific, medical, or legal documents? Would the SVM classifier for proposition filtering trained on educational topics generalize to other domains? Pilot studies on different domains would assess generalizability and broaden the applicability of the methodology.
- What is the cumulative error rate through the corpus creation pipeline? How do errors in proposition extraction (Open IE 4) propagate through SVM filtering, crowdsourcing, and expert annotation? Which types of errors (false positives, false negatives, incorrect argument boundaries) have the largest impact on final corpus quality? Error propagation analysis would improve understanding of corpus quality and identify opportunities for pipeline improvements.

Transparency:
The paper is generally transparent about methodology and corpus creation pipeline, with clear documentation of quality checkpoints and error analysis at each step. However, the paper does not explicitly discuss limitations of the core motivation claim (C1) or acknowledge that it relies on prior user studies without direct validation in this work. The paper does not validate automatic evaluation metrics against human judgments or acknowledge this as a gap. The paper does not explain the lower test-retest correlation for comparison tasks (0.69-0.72) compared to Likert tasks (0.73-0.82). The paper does not analyze error propagation through the corpus creation pipeline, despite documenting error rates at individual steps. The paper is transparent about the simplicity of the baseline system but does not discuss implications for task difficulty assessment.

Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: been intensively studied and is well represented in research literature. We report related work in the Section 2.1. Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: been intensively studied and is well represented in research literature. We report related work in the Section 2.1. Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: been intensively studied and is well represented in research literature. We report related work in the Section 2.1. Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

Below we describe the primary characteristics of a technical extractive summary and we present diﬀerent types of input texts that we used for the production of extractive summaries. 1.1.1 Technical Extractive Summaries In the case of multi-document summarization, the goal is to produce a readable presenta- tion of multiple documents, whereas in the case of technical summary creation, the goal is to convey the key features and basic underpinnings of a particular ﬁeld, early and late developments, important contributions and ﬁndings, contradicting positions that may re- verse trends or start new sub-ﬁelds, and basic deﬁnitions and examples that enable rapid understanding of a ﬁeld by non-experts. A prototypical example of a technical summary is that of “chapter notes,” i.e., short (50–500 word) descriptions of sub-areas found at the end of chapters of textbooks, such as Jurafsky and Martin’s (2008). Categorization or Classification Categorization involves identifying the main themes of a document by placing the document into a predefined set of topics (either as taxonomies or ontologies). Categorization only counts words that appear and, from the counts, identifies the main topics that the document covers. Categorization often relies on relationships identified by looking for broad terms, narrower terms, synonyms, and related terms. Categorization tools normally have a method for ranking the documents in order of which documents have the most content on a particular topic [10]. Another method is to represent topics as thematic graphs, and using a degree of similarity (or distance from the “reference” graph) to classify documents under a given category [11]. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: been intensively studied and is well represented in research literature. We report related work in the Section 2.1. Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

Below we describe the primary characteristics of a technical extractive summary and we present diﬀerent types of input texts that we used for the production of extractive summaries. 1.1.1 Technical Extractive Summaries In the case of multi-document summarization, the goal is to produce a readable presenta- tion of multiple documents, whereas in the case of technical summary creation, the goal is to convey the key features and basic underpinnings of a particular ﬁeld, early and late developments, important contributions and ﬁndings, contradicting positions that may re- verse trends or start new sub-ﬁelds, and basic deﬁnitions and examples that enable rapid understanding of a ﬁeld by non-experts. A prototypical example of a technical summary is that of “chapter notes,” i.e., short (50–500 word) descriptions of sub-areas found at the end of chapters of textbooks, such as Jurafsky and Martin’s (2008). Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
